OK-2026-HB1381.s: The measure would have required the Oklahoma Alcoholic Beverage Laws Enforcement Commission to make an annual report by February 28 that lists license revocations or suspensions, complaints, and ticket and penalty totals. It would also have required the report to be given to state leaders and posted on the commission’s website.

OK-2026-HB3004.s: The measure would extend the sunset date for the Oklahoma Board of Examiners in Optometry from July 1, 2026, to July 1, 2031. It affects the board that licenses and oversees optometrists in Oklahoma. It would take effect July 1, 2026, but also says it is an emergency and takes effect right away after passage and approval.

OK-2026-HB3021.s: The measure changes Oklahoma school curriculum and graduation rules, including a set 23-unit course plan for students in grades 8 through 12 starting in the 2025-2026 school year. It also changes some graduation paths, adds rules for online course waivers and school website notice, and lets certain military children meet the Oklahoma history requirement with a project or paper. State education and higher education agencies must also work together on a joint plan so courses meet graduation rules, and the measure was approved by the Governor.

OK-2026-HB3521.s: The act creates a new state law for money transmission services and replaces the old rules. It requires most money transmission businesses to get a license, and it sets rules for applications, renewals, records, funds, and state oversight. It also creates felony penalties for some false records or for doing licensed money transmission work without a license.

OK-2026-HB3880.s: The measure changes rules for the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Department’s Oklahoma Today Magazine division. It lets some employees earn extra pay as a commission for bringing in ad, sponsor, subscription, and related sales, with limits set in the bill. It became law without the governor’s signature and takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-HB3940.s: The bill changed several Oklahoma National Guard rules, including pay, retention bonuses, eligibility for CareerTech help, and museum funding. It would let certain compensation be paid from the Oklahoma National Guard Supplemental Retention Pay Revolving Fund, and it also changes how some Guard funds and museum funds are named and used. It became law on May 13, 2026, without the governor's signature.

OK-2026-HB4191.s: The measure changes Oklahoma’s Small Employer Quality Jobs Act by updating key definitions and the rules for getting incentive payments. It adds a definition for qualifying capital investment, which includes new construction, renovation, or new machinery bought after an application date, and it changes some job and eligibility tests for small employers. The bill became law on May 13, 2026.

OK-2026-HB4423.s: The bill would require the Oklahoma Health Care Authority to check Medicaid applicants through a federal immigration status system before benefits are given. If a person’s status cannot be verified, the Authority would notify the Attorney General, who would review the case and notify Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It would also require the Authority to post notice on its website and application portal about this review process. The bill would take effect October 1, 2026.

OK-2026-HB4432.s: The measure would change Oklahoma tax law on wagering losses, removing a limit on itemizing those losses for certain tax years. It would affect taxpayers who claim wagering losses on their state taxes. The bill also updates some tax law wording and references.

OK-2026-HCR1030.s: This resolution sets the lawmaking calendar for the 61st Oklahoma Legislature. It gives dates for when bills and joint resolutions must be drafted, introduced, passed in each chamber, and when each regular session must adjourn. It also says the schedule does not apply to certain measures, such as some agency rule, ethics, local law, pension, and budget bills.

OK-2026-HJR1023.s: The resolution approves a new workers' compensation fee schedule, which sets maximum rates paid to medical providers. It also directs copies to be sent to the Workers' Compensation Commission, the Governor, and the Secretary of State. It became law on May 13, 2026, and it is set to take effect on July 1, 2026, with an emergency declared.

OK-2026-HJR1088.s: A joint resolution approved certain permanent rules from several Oklahoma education agencies, including the State Department of Education, higher education, teacher retirement, charter schools, and career and technology education. The rules covered are those filed on or before February 1, 2026. It also directs the Secretary of State to send copies to the Governor and to the editor of The Oklahoma Register.

OK-2026-HJR1091.s: This joint resolution approved most permanent rules from several Oklahoma business and commerce agencies. It also approved the New Motor Vehicle Commission rules with one wording change, and excluded some proposed building code changes. The Secretary of State was directed to send copies to the Governor and the Oklahoma Register.

OK-2026-HJR1095.s: This joint resolution approved permanent rules for several Oklahoma state agencies, including Aerospace and Aeronautics, Consumer Credit, Transportation, Veterans Affairs, Securities, the State Election Board, and public employee retirement. It also approved Office of Management and Enterprise Services rules, except for certain major rule changes listed in the measure. The Secretary of State was directed to send copies to the Governor and the editor of The Oklahoma Register.

OK-2026-HJR1099.s: This joint resolution approves two proposed major rules for the Oklahoma Health Care Authority. It also directs the state secretary to send copies to the governor and the Oklahoma Register editor.

OK-2026-HJR1100.s: The resolution approves several proposed major rule changes from the Office of Management and Enterprise Services. It also directs the Oklahoma Secretary of State to send copies to the governor and the editor of The Oklahoma Register. It was approved by the governor on May 20, 2026.

OK-2026-HJR1101.s: This joint resolution would approve several proposed permanent rules for the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority. It would also direct the Oklahoma Secretary of State to send copies of the resolution to the governor and the editor of The Oklahoma Register.

OK-2026-HR1060.s: The resolution says the Oklahoma House should impeach Chief Justice Dustin Rowe of the Oklahoma Supreme Court. It says the basis is his conduct in relation to grand jury proceedings in Payne County, including claims of neglect of duty and corruption in office. It is a formal statement asking for impeachment under the Oklahoma Constitution.

OK-2026-SB1061.s: The law changes rules for mortgage brokers, mortgage lenders, and mortgage loan originators in Oklahoma. It defines a term used in the law, lets the agency use a national licensing system to handle records and fee payments, and updates license renewal rules. It also sets or updates several fees, including a $1,200 application fee for broker or lender licenses and a $150 fee for each branch office or extra trade name. It became law on 05/14/2026.

OK-2026-SB1090.s: The measure would change Oklahoma rules for the "Invest In Oklahoma" program, which lets public money be invested in private equity, venture capital, and growth funds. It would give the State Treasurer more of the job of picking and overseeing funds, set factors to use in that review, and require lists and reports on the program. It would also let certain state retirement and trust funds invest up to 5% of their assets in approved funds.

OK-2026-SB1191.s: The measure repeals the law that set up the Oklahoma Low Carbon Energy Initiative Board. It became law and takes effect on November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1216.s: Oklahoma’s drug court rules would be updated to change who can be considered for the program and how eligibility is reviewed. It keeps the focus on people with certain felony or misdemeanor charges and substance use issues, and it adds or restates the forms, notices, hearings, and plea steps tied to program entry. The act became law without the governor’s signature and takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB122.s: The bill would give $9 million to the Weigh Station Improvement Revolving Fund for the Oklahoma Department of Transportation to carry out its duties. It would take effect July 1, 2025. The measure has passed the Senate and was sent to the House.

OK-2026-SB1224.s: The measure lets the Pardon and Parole Board send notices to victims or their representatives by email if they have given an email address. It also keeps rules for sharing pardon and commutation applications, hearing schedules, and board decisions with victims, district attorneys, and others involved in the case. The act takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1257.s: The bill would change Oklahoma's drug law by updating the list of controlled substances in Schedules I and III. It adds one substance, removes one substance, and updates related wording in the law's definitions. These changes would affect people who make, sell, prescribe, or use these substances under state law.

OK-2026-SB1264.s: Approved by the governor, this measure changes which crimes are grouped as Class A3 and Class B3 offenses in Oklahoma. It adds and lists specific crimes in those groups, including some assault, abuse, arson, riot, forgery, and terrorism offenses. The text says the new class lists apply on or after January 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1286.s: The bill requires certain school districts and towns or cities that held an election run by a county election board on or after January 1, 2023, to provide a room to use as a polling place if there is no suitable one nearby and the county election board asks for it in writing. The space must be in a school or municipal building and must be provided at no cost. It was approved by the governor and takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1319.s: The bill would set up a process for homeowners to ask for help when their home is contaminated by substances like brine or oil that fall under the Corporation Commission’s power. It would create a Remediation Assistance Revolving Fund to pay for cleanup, stopping the contamination, and in some cases buying the property at fair market value. Cities or counties could hold the property, help remove a residence if needed, and return sale money to the fund. The measure was approved by the governor and takes effect as an emergency law.

OK-2026-SB1326.s: The measure changes rules for self-storage liens and rental agreements in Oklahoma. It lets rental agreements be sent and accepted by email if both sides agree, and it says an occupant’s rent payment or continued use can count as acceptance if the person does not sign within 30 days after the agreement is delivered. It also sets rules for towing vehicles after 60 days of unpaid rent and for notice before stored property can be treated as abandoned. It becomes effective November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB133.s: The bill would require people who want to use groundwater for a medical marijuana grow facility to show a valid commercial grower license to the Oklahoma Water Resources Board. It would keep the normal groundwater permit process in place for these users. The act would take effect July 1, 2025, and it includes an emergency clause.

OK-2026-SB1338.s: The bill would create a new state fund for the Education Department to award competitive grants for education projects that aim to improve student learning in Oklahoma. The State Board of Education would review and score grant applications, and the names of applicants would be removed before review. The fund could take in state money, gifts, grants, donations, and bequests, and the act would take effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1360.s: Oklahoma would change math instruction rules in public schools and create an Office of Mathematics Improvement in the State Department of Education. It would give teachers access to training, set rules for student math screening, and require schools to use a screening tool starting in the 2027-2028 school year. The measure would also change how math money is sent to districts and add funding for intervention services and district math improvement incentives. It was approved by the governor.

OK-2026-SB1437.s: The measure would direct the state Education Department to set rules for schools to give students a Presidential Fitness Test and base those rules on federal fitness advice. School districts would have to give the test once the rules are in place, with training for staff, exemptions for some students, and a parent or guardian opt-out option. Schools would use the results to encourage daily exercise and healthy habits, and the law would take effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1448.s: This law changes the list of cases that are exempt from the Oklahoma Consumer Protection Act. It affects publishers, broadcasters, printers, retailers acting in good faith, and some actions covered by other state or federal rules, as well as certain tax collections. It takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1451.s: The measure changes Oklahoma voter registration forms by adding a place for people to list prior voter registration in another county or state. It also says a signed registration form counts as a request to cancel any old registration, and county election boards must cancel a voter’s registration after getting notice of a new registration in another county or state. It also requires the state election board to send out a yearly electronic report with counts of certain voter registration notices and cancellations.

OK-2026-SB1531.s: The law gives the Oklahoma Department of Aerospace and Aeronautics more power to manage unmanned aircraft systems and advanced air mobility, which means new air tech and the needed support systems. It lets the department keep registries, study other states’ rules, apply for grants and test sites, and work with cities, counties, tribes, federal agencies, and other groups on infrastructure and testing. It also lets the department make rules to carry out the program. It takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1534.s: The bill would change Oklahoma rules for charities that ask for donations. It would update registration and reporting rules, set filing fees, and require certain contact and tax information to be filed with the Secretary of State. It would also change some rules for charitable nonprofit corporations, including who can serve on boards and certain actions they may not take.

OK-2026-SB1555.s: The bill would change a state law on Medicaid home- and community-based services by updating the definition of certain terms, including "developmental disability" and "individual with intellectual disability." It would also update some statutory language and take effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1557.s: The bill moves licensing for applied behavior analysis from the Department of Human Services to the State Board of Examiners of Psychologists. It would require applicants to meet set qualifications and pass a national criminal history record check, and the board would handle complaints and set renewal fees. It also keeps some school district workers and pilot project participants exempt, and it takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1589.s: The measure would update Oklahoma gambling law by defining online casino games and “representative of value,” which means money or credits that can be traded for prizes or cash. It would broaden the gambling offense to cover opening, running, or helping online casino games, including by suppliers, platform providers, promoters, and media affiliates. It would keep the offense as a Class C2 felony with a fine of $500 to $2,000 and would take effect on November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1595.s: State agencies and related groups would be barred from giving specific advice for or against a commercial driver training school. They also could not withhold student grants based on a student’s choice of school. Affected schools or students could sue if these rules are broken, and the act would take effect July 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1614.s: The bill would make Oklahoma’s teacher induction program state-supported and require every school district to take part starting in the 2026-2027 school year. It would keep the program focused on helping first-year teachers with training, mentors, and coaching, and it would allow funding from state money, grants, and outside groups. The State Board of Education could also write rules for the program. It would take effect on July 1, 2026, and was passed with an emergency clause.

OK-2026-SB1632.s: The bill would have the State Department of Education approve career-readiness tests and related credentials for public school students. Starting in the 2026-2027 school year, these tests would be available to students in grades 10 through 12, and districts could give them at no cost to students who choose to take them. It also lets state higher education officials write rules so colleges may give credit for these test results and credentials; the bill was approved by the governor and takes effect July 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1670.s: The measure would require the Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education to add a tiered ownership system to a model policy for higher education. It affects higher education schools and the state regents that set the policy.

OK-2026-SB1775.s: Oklahoma municipalities would have clearer rules for fines and fee-in-lieu-of-fine amounts in local ordinances. If a city sets a penalty above the maximum allowed for the same offense under state law or other law, the extra amount would be void and cut back to the lawful limit. The bill became law on May 12, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1796.s: This law lets foster parents in Oklahoma use approved alternate caregivers, respite care, and short informal care plans for foster children. It sets time limits, including up to 14 consecutive days for an alternate caregiver and up to 72 hours for informal care, and requires notice to the Department of Human Services. It also requires checks, home review, and approval for alternate caregivers and respite families, and it takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB1859.s: The measure would create a Cyber Crime and Fraud Unit within the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation to handle cybercrime, digital evidence, and fraud cases. It would let the Bureau assign staff and resources to the unit, make rules for it, and work with other law enforcement agencies. It would also set up a revolving fund for the unit to use for its work. It was approved by the governor.

OK-2026-SB1877.s: This law requires many state agencies and offices to send certain reports through one central filing system run by the Office of the Secretary of State. It also removes some old reports and updates several state laws tied to areas like children, courts, health, public finance, and motor vehicles. It affects agencies and others who must file those reports.

OK-2026-SB1894.s: The bill would change the cap on required teacher professional development hours in a five-year period. It would also keep the current training rules for topics like child abuse reporting, autism, and dyslexia, and it would require school districts to report their training needs, costs, and results to the state. The act would have taken effect July 1, 2026, with an emergency clause for immediate effect upon passage and approval.

OK-2026-SB2.s: The bill would set new distance rules for wind energy projects in Oklahoma. It would require wind towers to be at least one-quarter mile from homes and from nonparticipating property after November 1, 2025, and it would keep other setback rules in place for airports, schools, hospitals, and military sites. It also would require proof of federal aviation review and cleared defense issues to be filed, with daily fines of up to $1,500 for violations.

OK-2026-SB2011.s: The bill updates Oklahoma’s assault and battery laws and changes which offenses count in certain crime classes. It expands the list of Class B5 and Class B6 offenses, including some attacks on police, correctional staff, service animals, and sex offender registration violations. The bill was approved by the governor and applies on or after January 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB2049.s: Oklahoma’s Department of Transportation would have to tell the Transportation Commission before it makes a claim against a surety company for losses tied to a contractor’s failure to perform. The commission would review the request and must approve it before the department can go ahead. The act was approved by the governor and takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB206.s: The measure says certain ambulance services count as essential services for federal funding purposes. It applies to ambulance services run by cities, counties, ambulance districts, tribal entities, or other public groups, and to some licensed 911 ambulance services that have a contract with them. It was approved by the governor and takes effect right away because it declares an emergency.

OK-2026-SB2063.s: The bill would change Oklahoma’s unclaimed property law. It would let the State Treasurer ask for more information in some claim cases, let claimants ask for a hearing in some cases, and require a response within a set time. It would also require certain deposit and fund information to be posted on a public website and made available at the end of each fiscal year.

OK-2026-SB2071.s: The measure would update parts of Oklahoma’s milk law, including some definitions and the rules for dairy inspection and grading programs. It would also keep the 1-cent fees on raw milk and Grade A milk products, and on milk brought in from other states, going to the state inspection fund. The act would take effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB2084.s: The measure sets a cap on payouts for wrongful termination claims against higher education institutions for faculty members. In those cases, the total paid to settle a claim, through settlement, arbitration, or court order, could not be more than two years of the faculty member’s base pay or contract benefits, and it would count back pay and other money damages. It would not count retirement contributions already earned or unpaid wages or leave already accrued. The act takes effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SB2182.s: Creates a state law that lets a person sue if someone intentionally shares or threatens to share a private intimate image without consent. It covers people shown in those images and sets rules for when consent, privacy, and certain defenses apply, including cases involving parents, legal guardians, cloud and hosting providers, and matters of public concern. The law also allows damages, court costs, attorney fees, and other relief, and it became law after the governor approved it.

OK-2026-SB237.s: The measure would change Oklahoma’s property tax break for qualifying manufacturing facilities. It would define a battery energy storage system and keep its cost from counting toward some investment tests for the exemption, while also limiting what counts as a manufacturing facility. It would affect businesses seeking or using that tax exemption.

OK-2026-SB258.s: The bill would create a state fund for the Oklahoma Department of Transportation to help counties pay for road and bridge projects on major collector routes. It would set up a grant program for counties, and projects would be ranked by things like safety, readiness, and how important the route is for public use. The act would take effect July 1, 2025, if enacted.

OK-2026-SB259.s: Approved by the governor, the measure changes how groundwater use is permitted, metered, reported, and checked in Oklahoma. It requires more reporting for permit holders, adds rules for some animal feeding operations, and lets the Water Resources Board investigate complaints and set fines or other penalties for waste. It also expands meter or measuring system use for wells that need a permit, and limits permits for some data center cooling systems unless they use lower-water cooling methods.

OK-2026-SB423.s: The bill would change how people can get copies of their medical records and medical bills from health care providers. It would set or raise some fees for copies, electronic records, x-rays, and records requested by lawyers, insurance companies, or by subpoena, and it would keep some special rules for mental health records and certain correctional records. It would also keep rules for sharing records in injury or death cases and for who can request records for a deceased patient.

OK-2026-SB540.s: Oklahoma would join the Dentist and Dental Hygienist Compact, which lets dentists and dental hygienists licensed in one participating state practice in another participating state under a compact privilege. It also lets the governor enter the compact with other states or jurisdictions that have joined it. The law sets up shared rules, data sharing, and background check steps for states in the compact.

OK-2026-SB563.s: The bill changes how county planning commissions and county boards of adjustment are set up. It would make the county commission chair, or a designee, a member of the planning commission, shorten member terms, and set the board of adjustment at three, five, or seven county resident property owners with shorter terms. It also lets county commissioners hire private legal counsel for the board of adjustment and says older county planning and zoning actions stay in effect until changed.

OK-2026-SB604.s: The measure updates Oklahoma rules for motor vehicle dealers, manufacturers, and related businesses. It changes some legal definitions, adds rules for dealer management system providers, and sets limits on when a dealer license can be denied, revoked, or suspended. It also changes rules on stopping or canceling a franchise agreement.

OK-2026-SB633.s: Approved by the governor, this law changes Oklahoma’s Children’s Code and child endangerment rules. It requires fentanyl testing in certain drug screenings, directs the Department of Human Services to seek consent for testing and to notify a district attorney in some cases, and creates a fund for child welfare fentanyl testing. It also changes when child endangerment applies and lets courts require some people to pay for drug testing, with some funding and reporting duties for the department.

OK-2026-SB647.s: The bill would change how cities and towns handle zoning and land-use decisions. It would require public notice and hearings, set rules for when proposed zoning changes need a higher vote, and say these decisions must be based on objective facts. It would also change court review of some city zoning decisions and appeals from boards of adjustment, and set new rules for planning commission review of plats and subdivisions.

OK-2026-SB667.s: The bill would require chiropractors to use the online licensure portal to apply for an original license. It would also change some license rules, including proof of education, exam steps, and how the board must notify an applicant if it denies the application. The bill also covers chiropractic care for animals and was approved by the governor.

OK-2026-SB904.s: The bill would bar state money, Medicaid coverage, and state buildings or facilities from being used for gender transition procedures for minors. It would also say that people already getting this care can keep receiving it if it started before the law takes effect. A state officer or employee who knowingly breaks the rule could be charged with a misdemeanor, and the law would take effect November 1, 2026.

OK-2026-SJR49.s: This joint resolution repeals certain permanent rules of the Oklahoma Wildlife Conservation Commission. It affects the commission’s rules in Oklahoma and was approved by the governor.

OK-2026-SJR52.s: This resolution approved certain permanent rules of the Oklahoma Health Care Authority, the state agency that runs some health care programs. It covers a set of rules listed in the measure, and it directs copies to be sent to the governor and the Oklahoma Register. It was approved by the governor on May 20, 2026.

OK-2026-SJR53.s: This joint resolution approves a set of permanent rules for the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority. It also directs the Secretary of State to send copies to the Governor and the Oklahoma Register, the state publication for official notices.
